Book burnings have traditionally been politically and religiously motivated. An attempt to suppress competing ideas or the evolution of culture as a means of social control. Today we do have another kind of book burning motivated by greed and the desire to capture and control the use of intellectual property for sake of profit.

College textbook publishers have long waged a war on their consumers and one of the fronts of this war is used books. They want used textbooks to disappear because they can make more money selling people new ones. But they adopted a tradition of rather durable book bindings that make the books rather long-lasting and escalated their prices to such an extreme that it really compels schools to reuse the books as long as they can and students to recover their costs on them if possible. So publishers have adopted the tactic of forcing the content of textbooks to become obsolete at ever-increasing rates. Books of certain subjects are naturally more or less resistant to obsolescence. Books in the fields of computers or astronomy go obsolete pretty rapidly because advances and discoveries in those fields are very frequent. But publishers have taken to making very superficial changes to all sorts of books to compel new editions and offer kickbacks to professors by various means to make them compel use of the new editions. And so the used books are forced into obsolescence and resale value drops to nothing. Some conscientious professors have resisted and protested this, but it's not easy when the kickbacks they might get can, in some cases, literally double their yearly incomes.

Given how frequently textbooks are replaced, it would seem logical that schools would embrace 'ebooks' for this. But they haven't been very popular in practice because the publishers refuse to let them truly compete in price with print books based on their naturally low marginal costs. The savings on an ebook might be, at best, 30%. And they have taken to other, more dystopian, practices with them. They often include DRM code that prevents their resale or gifting to others or even makes the books self-destruct after a single semester of use. Increasingly, companies don't want you to own anything and would rather you rent everything and publishers are the worst in this. They have been systematically seeking every possible angle they can to whittle-away at consumer rights in order to control consumer behavior to their ends.

But on the positive side, ebooks are an ideal way to make an end-run around this expanding control through the publishing of open source textbooks. The content of textbooks originates in the academic community. They create it. But it fell into the hands of corporations because, as countries took to expanding access to higher education in their societies, schools could no longer manage the now industrial mass production of books. They had to turn it over to industrialists. Ebooks have no such problem. They take no 'industry' to produce and have zero marginal cost. They could return control of textbook publishing back to the schools and academic communities themselves and allow them to create 'living books' that would be perpetually and automatically updated like any other software as advances were made in their fields, not sold in series of obsolescent editions. But professors are fuddy-duddies who are set in their ways and mostly rather computer illiterate. And it's very hard to resist the lure of those kickbacks and gifts from publishers. One top US textbook publisher boasted a 2 billion dollar per year marketing budget. Have you ever seen an ad for a textbook?
